name: Umar Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter. We build the timber and steel moulds that the concrete gets poured into, for floors, columns, stair cores. Right now I'm on a seven-storey office block by the ring road, for a contractor called Carrow and Sons. Start at seven, finish at half four, home by half five if the traffic's kind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pour days. You spend a week building a deck, the pump turns up, and by lunch there's a floor where there was nothing. What wears me out is winter, honestly, standing on a deck in the wind at seven in the morning. I don't do any of the AI stuff. My cousin Rafi keeps showing me apps on his phone, and I tell him I've got a tape measure and a pencil and they've never once crashed on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone was going on about AI like it was the end of the world, and it turns out it writes emails a bit quicker. On site nobody would even notice, the concrete still needs a mould.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which is what I'd want. The job's steady as long as people keep building offices and car parks. Concrete doesn't care how clever the computer is, somebody still has to build the box it goes in. My real worry is the same as always, that a big job finishes and the next one is two months away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing. I'd keep putting two hundred a month aside towards a deposit on a flat, which I've been doing for three years now. Maybe I'd do my next ticket for working at height when it runs out, but that's just normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I've got about four months put away, the gang's good and Marek, our gang leader, always finds the next job. It's the life I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned gaps between jobs. Has that happened to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, two years ago, five weeks between the hospital car park and the next job. I lived on savings and did a bit of fencing for a mate. It wasn't nice but I got through it, and that's why I keep the money there now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your cousin Rafi say if he heard you say AI was hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafi would laugh and say I'd just got lucky. He does deliveries and uses an app for his whole route, so for him it's not hype at all. We'd argue about it over Sunday dinner at my mum's, same as always.

say: AI turned out to **write emails** faster and not much else.
On site **nobody would notice**, because concrete still needs a mould.
think: **Nothing changing** is exactly what he wants for his job.
His real worry is the **gap between jobs**, not technology.
do: Keep putting **two hundred a month** aside for a flat deposit.
Renew his **working-at-height ticket** when it runs out, as usual.
feel: **Calm**, with four months saved and a good gang leader finding work.
S0.quote: Concrete doesn't care how clever the computer is, somebody still has to build the box it goes in.
fieldNote: He's proud of **not using AI** and frames it as reliability.
A past **five-week gap** between jobs shapes how he saves.
Feels most secure trusting **people he knows**, like his gang leader.

steps.text: Keep working formwork for Carrow and Sons on the office block
Put two hundred a month aside towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't touch us much. Robots are slow to come onto sites, and a formwork deck is a mess of timber, props and rain. I'd probably say that down the pub, that the office lot should worry, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking about it properly, it does bother me a bit. I build offices, and if half the people in offices are getting replaced by software, who needs a new seven-storey office block? If AI empties the offices, I'm the one who loses the job building the next office. That's not something I'd say on site, because the lads would think I'd gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and see how it pans out, honestly. I wouldn't do any courses yet, because I don't know what would be worth doing. I'd keep saving, and I'd listen to Marek, because if the office jobs dry up he'll know first which contractors are still pouring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine today, but I'd be looking at the cranes around town and counting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the work moved from offices to other kinds of building, could you follow it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, formwork is formwork. Hospitals, flood walls, railway bridges, it's all concrete. I just don't like moving firms, I've been with Carrow for six years and I know where everything is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the AI tools Rafi shows you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the one that reads drawings, if the whole gang was using it and Marek said it was worth it. I wouldn't be the first. I'd want to see it work on a real pour before I trusted it.

say: The changes **hit offices**, not formwork gangs on muddy decks.
Robots are **slow to arrive** on messy building sites.
think: Fewer office workers could mean **fewer office blocks** for him to build.
He'd keep this worry private so the gang doesn't think he's **gone soft**.
do: Hold off on any **courses** until it's clear what's worth doing.
Keep **saving** for the deposit at the same rate.
Ask the gang leader which **contractors** are still pouring concrete.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching the cranes around town and counting them.
S1.quote: If AI empties the offices, I'm the one who loses the job building the next office.
fieldNote: He sees the risk through **demand for buildings**, not through robots.
Public toughness hides a **private worry** he won't share on site.
Prefers **staying put** with one firm, even if he could follow the work.

steps.text: Stay on the formwork gang at Carrow and Sons
Hold off on courses until it's clear which ones pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, letting it all happen at once with nobody ready. I'm not a political person, but I'd say somebody in charge should have slowed it down. At work I'd probably keep my head down and not say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's bad for me, and fast. In 2028 the offices empty, so by 2029 nobody's ordering new office blocks, and that's my whole job. Then in 2031 robots that can build formwork turn up anyway. Two years isn't enough time for a man who still writes his measurements on a bit of plywood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the deposit plan and keep the money as a cushion, because a flat is no good if I can't pay the mortgage. I'd give notice on my place and move back in with my mum in Westgate to save the eight hundred a month rent. I'd ask Marek about any government jobs, like the flood defences on the river, because public money might keep flowing when private money stops. And I'd stop eating out and cancel the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, if I'm honest. I'd be lying awake. I'm not good at learning new things off a screen and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at learning off a screen. Would you try anyway, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but I'd be slow, and the young lads would beat me to it. My cousin Rafi would help me, he's patient. I'd still rather find a job doing what I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back in with your mum actually be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, at twenty-seven. My mum would be pleased, she'd feed me every night and ask why I'm not married. But I'd save nearly a thousand a month between rent and food, and that's what matters if the work stops.

say: Letting it all happen **at once** with nobody ready is madness.
He'd **keep his head down** at work and say little.
think: Empty offices mean **no new office blocks**, which is his whole job.
Two years is far **too short** for someone who avoids screens.
do: Drop the **deposit plan** and keep the savings as a cushion.
Move back to **his mum's** house to save eight hundred a month rent.
Chase **public projects** like river flood defences through his gang leader.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep, knowing he's slow with new technology.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for a man who still writes his measurements on a bit of plywood.
fieldNote: He expects demand for his work to **collapse** before robots even arrive.
His **resistance to screens** becomes a source of real fear here.
Family is his **safety net**: his mum's house and his patient cousin.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and stop eating out
Ask cousin Rafi for help learning job apps
Look for formwork on public flood defence and bridge jobs
Give up the rented flat and move back to his mum's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so don't panic. Five years is a long time on a building site, that's three or four big jobs. I'd say it to the younger lads who'd start getting jumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gives me until about 2031 before the office work dries up, and then robots in 2034, when I'm thirty-five. Five years of warning is long enough to see the job going, but I'd still wait until I saw it with my own eyes. I'm not proud of that, but it's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving, maybe push it up to three hundred a month. Around 2029, if offices really are emptying, I'd ask Carrow to put me on their infrastructure jobs, the bridges and the rail work. I'd keep the deposit money but I wouldn't buy anything until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lying awake like the fast one, but it's on my mind every time a job finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see to stop waiting and act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job cancelled. If Carrow loses an office job because the client pulls out, that's my sign. Marek would know first, he always hears it at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until you saw it, but you'd also ask to move to bridges. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. Asking Carrow to move me to bridges isn't really changing anything, it's the same firm and the same work. That's the kind of move I can make without feeling like I'm jumping off a cliff.

say: Five years is **three or four** big jobs, so don't panic.
He'd calm the **younger lads** who start getting jumpy.
think: Office work dries up around **2031** and robots reach formwork around 2034.
He knows he'd **wait to see it** before acting, and isn't proud of it.
do: Raise deposit saving to **three hundred** a month.
Ask Carrow for a move to **infrastructure jobs** around 2029.
Hold off on **buying a flat** until things are clearer.
feel: **Anxious** whenever a job finishes, though not losing sleep.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is long enough to see the job going, but I'd still wait until I saw it with my own eyes.
fieldNote: He names his own **wait-and-see** habit with honesty.
His trigger to act is a **cancelled job**, something he can see.
Public projects look like his **escape route** from office building.

steps.text: Raise deposit saving from two hundred to three hundred a month
Hold off buying a flat until office work is clearer
Ask Carrow to move him onto bridge and rail jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lifetime in construction, and half of these predictions never happen. I'd probably say it with a laugh. At work it wouldn't change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine for most of it. Robots for hands-on work around 2039, I'd be forty, so I'd have done a good stretch. At forty I'd be too old to start again and too young to stop, and that's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep going for now. I'd buy the flat, because I'd have years of wages to pay it down. I'd keep an eye out in the second half of the ten years and think about a supervisor ticket then, if it looked like the office jobs were going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far off, so I can push it to the back of my mind, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat. Wouldn't that tie you down if the work dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'm not renting forever. With ten years I could pay off a good chunk. My mum always says you buy the roof first and worry about the weather later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start preparing earlier than the second half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A gang leader I trust getting laid off, or a job where they bring a robot on site for the decks. If I saw that with my own eyes, I'd sign up for a course the next week.

say: Ten years is a **lifetime** in construction, and predictions often fail.
At work, it **wouldn't change** a thing.
think: He'd get a **good stretch** of work before robots around 2039.
Being **forty** when robots arrive feels too old to start again.
do: **Buy the flat** and pay it down with years of steady wages.
Consider a **supervisor ticket** in the second half of the decade.
feel: **Uneasy**, though he can push it to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: At forty I'd be too old to start again and too young to stop, and that's what bothers me.
fieldNote: The long warning lets him **put off** any change, which suits him.
His mum's saying about **buying the roof** first guides his money choice.
Quietly aware that **age forty** is an awkward point to be replaced.

steps.text: Keep working formwork with the same gang
Buy a flat with the deposit savings
Decide on a supervisor ticket after about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is if the government kept building things, bridges, hospitals, flood walls, so there's still concrete to pour while everyone works it out. Pay me to build a flood wall and I'll learn whatever you want on the weekends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the older lads. Marek's fifty-one, and he's the best formwork man I know. If it all goes quickly, nobody's retraining Marek.

headlineQuote: Pay me to build a flood wall and I'll learn whatever you want on the weekends.
portrait: Umar is a 27-year-old **formwork carpenter** building office blocks, renting alone and saving for a flat.
He **never uses AI** and is proud of trusting his tape measure and pencil.
He sees the danger through **empty offices** meaning fewer offices to build.
In fast scenarios he'd **move back** to his mum's and chase public building work.
With more warning, he admits he'd **wait and see** until a job got cancelled.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because office building stops before he can adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Steady **public building work** like bridges and flood walls to keep crews employed.
Weekend **retraining** alongside paid work, not instead of it.
